title: After COP31 setback, EU lawmakers greenlight carbon permit compromise
content:
A deal struck by EU negotiators in October has cleared its next hurdle, with the European Parliament voting to raise the threshold for cancelling surplus carbon permits from 400 to 700 million. The change aims to make the EU carbon market more flexible and predictable for industry.

The European Parliament approved on Tuesday changes to the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The agreement passed with 403 votes in favour, 78 against, and 146 abstentions.

Speaking ahead of the vote, Parliament’s rapporteur, MEP Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D/ITA), recalled the failure of COP31. It was, he noted, the first UN climate conference since 2009 to end without an agreement.

“Now, more than ever, Europe’s leadership is essential. But we are only credible if our ambition is matched by an effective instrument that transforms our economy. EU ETS is a good example of that,” he said.

Operating since 2019, the Market Stability Reserve absorbs surplus emission allowances and releases them when the market faces shortages. Under current rules, allowances held in the reserve above 400 million are permanently cancelled.

title: Europe is working more than ever, yet millions are still trapped in poverty. What does the EU advise?
content:
Despite record employment, the EU has cut the number of people at risk of poverty by less than a quarter of its 2030 target. The European Commission is urging governments to invest in people’s skills, create better jobs and strengthen competitiveness — while keeping public budgets in check.

The EU set its target in 2021, committing to lift at least 15 million people out of poverty or social exclusion by 2030 compared with 2019 levels. Until 2025, however, the number fell by just 3.5 million. With five years left, the bloc must make up remaining 11.5 million. That would require progress at roughly three times the pace achieved so far.

Meanwhile, higher energy prices are fuelling inflation, house prices continue to climb sharply across many member states, and borrowing costs are increasing. These are among the findings of the European Commission’s 2027 European Semester Autumn Package, presented on Tuesday, which sets out the bloc’s economic, social and employment priorities for the coming year.

While the EU is approaching its 2030 target of a 78 per cent employment rate, higher employment figures do not tell the whole story.

title: Electric cars pull ahead. Brussels puts brakes on imported hybrids
content:
Europeans are buying electric cars at record speed. Yet Brussels is busy protecting a different technology. From December, the EU will cap imports of hybrid cars, while lawmakers consider keeping hybrids and combustion engines on sale after 2035.

For many drivers, the maths has changed. A home-charged electric car now costs about half as much to run as a petrol or diesel one, according to the green group Transport & Environment (T&E). Cheaper models are arriving too. T&E expects sales of electric cars under €25,000 to rise sevenfold this year compared with 2024.

The shift shows in the latest figures. Between January and October, almost one in four new cars registered in the EU ran on batteries alone, the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) reported on Tuesday. Electric cars also outsold petrol models over the period. Hybrids, however, remain the most popular choice.

title: Greece ditched coal in 15 years. The rest of Europe could learn from it
content:
Greece has shown that ditching coal need not be painful. Just 15 years ago, coal accounted for more than half of its electricity generation. Today, only one coal-fired unit remains, with gas, wind, solar and hydropower taking its place. Could Greece offer a blueprint for the rest of the EU?

As Greek Minister of Environment and Energy Stavros Papastavrou acknowledges, the southern European country is still recovering from the consequences of the financial crisis that hit in the first half of the previous decade. Despite this, it is pressing ahead with ambitious energy projects, often with financial support from the European Union. These include a subsea cable to Egypt, imports of natural gas from the eastern Mediterranean and connecting the Greek islands to the mainland electricity grid.

Speaking to journalists, Minister Papastavrou said that Crete and the Cyclades islands had already been connected to the mainland grid. Other islands are due to follow in the coming years.

title: Survival vs. combat: Freedom of movement in High North becomes logistics problem
content:
Snow-bound Nordic forces risk stalling. The EU’s Military Mobility Package will help, but cannot fix the issue alone.

In the High North, movement is never guaranteed. Snow, ice, and steep terrain turn short distances into obstacles. Freezing temperatures challenge vehicles, equipment, and the people who rely on them. The harder test is not reaching a destination. It is staying mobile, supplied, and effective; all this far from anything you would normally call infrastructure.

You have to be able to switch from wheels to tracks on the field, even if it’s minus 10 degrees.
— Lt Col David Bonne, French High Mountain Military School Bonne

title: Brussels wants greener fishing. Its own rules are standing in the way
content:
Outdated EU rules are preventing fishers from modernising their fleets and investing in cleaner technology, national governments warn. They are calling for more ambitious reforms than Brussels is currently willing to offer.

European governments are urging Brussels to revise fishing rules that they say prevent the modernisation of fishing businesses. The EU Commission, however, has opted to take a partial approach to revision. The debate emerged during the Council meeting where ministers assessed the Commission Vision 2040 for fisheries and aquaculture.

The goal of the Vision is to protect the EU marine ecosystems, boost seafood production and support coastal communities. But several countries said these goals are meaningless unless actual changes were made to the rules.

European Commission’s Vision 2040 identifies its priorities for the next 15 years. These include cleaner fishing vessels, stronger support for small-scale fishers and increased public investment in aquaculture.

title: Costa’s EU budget cut meets chorus of doubt, reservations
content:
The proposed 10-per-cent cut has drawn fire from Paris and the largest parliamentary group. It has also earned scepticism from Berlin and the Commission, which welcome it as the “first step” only.

The European Parliament’s largest political group has rejected European Council President António Costa’s proposal to cut the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework by roughly 10 per cent. The group’s chief negotiator called the offer unacceptable. The EPP Group has 185 members from all member states.

MEP Siegfried Mureșan (EPP/ROU), the group’s vice-president, reacted to Mr Costa’s negotiating box. “President Costa’s proposal is simply unacceptable. The Council is fixated on cuts when Europe needs ambition and resources to tackle its mounting challenges.” Mr Mureșan went further. “The Council is moving further away from Parliament’s position. It must change course.”

He warned national leaders not to expect easy approval. “National leaders must not expect the European Parliament to rubber-stamp a budget that holds Europe back.” He wants a moderate 10 per cent increase, backed by efficient new own resources, including a digital levy that would make tech giants pay.

title: Ceasefire first, Brussels insists as Washington links Ukraine’s security to Europe’s
content:
Ukraine’s guarantees come with a condition: Donald Trump would support them only if they served America’s national interests. His negotiators now want to fold them into a much wider deal on Europe’s post-war security.

Talks on Europe’s future security architecture can only begin once a ceasefire is in place in Ukraine, the European Commission insists. Its position comes in response to a new proposal from US negotiator Jared Kushner, who wants to link security guarantees for Kyiv to a broader post-war settlement in Europe.

“Our position has not changed,” Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said. “Those discussions need to take place in the appropriate forum, meaning with NATO allies and with the EU member states fully involved.”

Brussels also confirmed that it remains in regular contact with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner over preparations for possible multilateral talks.

Mr Kushner set out the US approach in more detail in a post on X on Sunday. He argued that the two issues are inseparable. “Security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture. The two must be considered together,” he wrote.

title: Did Coca-Cola bottler stop cheaper drinks from crossing EU borders?
content:
A can of Coke is the same in Madrid and Amsterdam. Its price may not be. Brussels wants to know whether Coca-Cola’s biggest European bottler stopped supermarkets from buying fizzy drinks where they are cheapest.

The suspicion is simple. Big supermarket chains operate across borders and want to buy drinks wherever the deal is best. The European Commission suspects that Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP) may have deliberately made that harder. On 23 November, it opened a formal antitrust investigation.

CCEP is the largest supplier of fizzy drinks in Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. The probe covers drinks that people buy in shops to take home. Restaurants, hotels, and cafés are not part of it.

Investigators will check whether CCEP offered retailers discounts only if the drinks stayed in the country. They will also look at whether it sold different bottle sizes in different countries to make resale harder. Two more practices are under scrutiny: rewards for retailers who limited imports into Spain, and a refusal to negotiate supply deals covering several countries at once.

title: ‘This will become mass surveillance’: Digital rights expert on Frontex’s social media plans
content:
Your social media posts could soon become a matter of EU border security. Under a new proposal, Frontex would monitor online content related to irregular migration, flag potentially illegal material and request its removal. “It will necessarily affect large numbers of people using social media,” warns Chloé Berthélémy of European Digital Rights in an interview with EU Perspectives.

The proposal follows the migration crisis in Ceuta, which the Commission says showed the need for Frontex to act before situations escalate. But giving a border agency eyes on people’s social media comes with serious implications for privacy and free speech. Chloé Berthélémy of European Digital Rights (EDRi) argues that the plan could amount to mass surveillance.

Since the reception crisis in 2015, the EU has committed itself to a policy of deterrence, aggression and incarceration against asylum seekers and migrants arriving in Europe. This has created a “Fortress Europe” that controls and militarises its borders to prevent, control and criminalise people moving across and between them.

title: Who skipped work for GTA VI? Dutch staff, young men, and US soldiers
content:
After 13 years of waiting, GTA VI finally went on sale on 19 November. Workers across Europe rushed to book the day off, many turning it into a four-day weekend. Meanwhile, Brussels is rethinking the rules for online games, from virtual currencies to child protection.

Grand Theft Auto VI, developed by Rockstar Games, arrived after two delays and countless internet jokes about things happening “before GTA VI”. The game takes players back to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida, modelled on Florida. But while it is set in America, the excitement is worldwide, with European gamers rearranging their schedules to play.

According to Remote, a global HR platform, annual-leave bookings for the release day were 32 per cent higher than for the same Thursday in 2025 worldwide, among employees on its platform. Several EU countries recorded increases, with the Netherlands leading the global ranking at 58 per cent, followed by Ireland at 50 per cent and Spain at 46 per cent. Portugal and Poland both recorded increases of 29 per cent, Italy 25 per cent and France five per cent.

title: Factory worker turned lawmaker: More money for industry is not a long-term solution for Europe
content:
Rudi Kennes fought to save Opel’s Antwerp factory before entering the European Parliament. Now, as lawmakers negotiate the Industrial Accelerator Act, the former factory worker and trade unionist wants guarantees that supporting European industry will also benefit its workers.

The Belgian lawmaker represents The Left in negotiations on the proposal as a shadow rapporteur. The Industrial Accelerator Act seeks to strengthen European production, making the debate over what qualifies as “Made in Europe” particularly important to him.

I do not think this will be a long-term solution for Europe. We might buy ourselves some time by giving the industry another few hundred million or billion euros. Structurally, though, I do not think that solves the problem.
— Rudi Kennes (Left/BE)

title: Can Europe stop bots from hijacking democracy without ending anonymity?
content:
One criminal network used 40,000 SIM cards to set up almost 50m fake online accounts. As Europe heads into a busy election year, lawmakers in Brussels are asking how to stop such bot armies without taking away people’s right to speak anonymously online.

With a string of national elections due across Europe in 2027, the stakes are rising. Fake accounts, coordinated disinformation campaigns, and online harassment are fuelling concerns across the EU. Yet lawmakers are divided over how to tackle manipulation without undermining anonymity and freedom of expression.

Bot farms and social media anonymity took centre stage in the European Parliament on 16 November. MEPs, Europol, and civil society representatives met at a hearing of the Special Committee on the European Democracy Shield (EUDS). They discussed how automated accounts distort political debate, amplify divisive content, and target public figures. What divided MEPs most was the line between anonymity and inauthenticity.

title: The US has the money, China has the speed. Europe’s €36.9bn health biotech needs both
content:
Medicines and vaccines are the fastest-growing part of Europe’s biotech economy, a new study shows. Yet European firms still go to Nasdaq when they need billions. Brussels hopes its Biotech Act will keep the next breakthroughs at home.

Healthcare biotechnology added €36.9bn to the EU economy in 2024. That is almost nine-tenths of the record €42.2bn generated by all biotech sectors together. And the figure leaves out the start-ups that are developing tomorrow’s medicines.

The numbers come from the latest edition of a study by the WifOR Institute, an independent research body, for EuropaBio, the European Association of Bioindustries. It tracks 117 biotech products in the 24 member states that make them, from 2008 to 2024.

The study splits biotech into three sectors: healthcare, industrial, and agricultural. Healthcare covers medicines and vaccines for people and animals, plus some ingredients made for medicine production.

Biotechnology continues as an economic powerhouse in the EU. — Claire Skentelbery, Director General, EuropaBio
